lede: Put resistors in a line and their resistances add up. Put them side by side and the total drops below the smallest of them. This topic turns both facts into calculations, from a simple sum to a circuit that mixes the two.
can: Add resistors in series and halve an equal pair in parallel
Find the resistance of any two resistors in parallel with the Higher equation
Reduce a circuit with series and parallel sections to a single resistance

md: Every resistor opposes the current a little. What matters to the supply is the total opposition it meets, and that depends on how the resistors are joined as well as on their values.

caption: Same battery, same two resistors: in a line the total goes up, side by side it goes down.

md: The **total resistance** is the single resistor that could replace all of them and draw the same current from the supply. Two 6 Ω resistors in a line give 12 Ω; side by side they give only 3 Ω.
**Read the figure.** The ammeter reads 0.50 A in series and 2.00 A in parallel: the smaller the total resistance, the bigger the current from the same battery.

prompt: A second resistor is connected in parallel with one already across a battery. What happens to the total resistance and to the current from the battery?
options: the total resistance falls and the current rises
the total resistance rises and the current falls
both stay the same, because the battery is the same
answer: the total resistance falls and the current rises
explain: A resistor added side by side is a second route for the charge, so more current flows from the same battery, and a bigger current for the same voltage means a smaller total resistance. That is the parallel half of the figure: 2.00 A against 0.50 A. The total falls and the current rises.

text: 2. Why series adds and parallel shrinks

md: In series the same current has to pass through every resistor in turn, and the supply voltage is shared among them. Each resistor adds its own opposition to the one route, so the resistances add.
In parallel each extra branch is another route. It has the full voltage across it, so it carries extra current; the total current rises, and the total resistance falls below even the smallest branch.

title: The check that catches most slips
md: Two resistors in parallel always combine to less than the smaller of the two. If a parallel answer comes out bigger than either resistor, something has gone wrong.

title: PhET: Circuit Construction Kit: DC

task: Connect one resistor across a battery with an ammeter in the main line and note the current. Predict the new reading, then add a second identical resistor in parallel and check. Finally put the two resistors in series instead and compare the three readings.

prompt: A 10 Ω resistor and a 40 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Which of these could be their combined resistance?
explain: Side by side, the pair gives the charge two routes, so the total must be less than the smaller resistor, 10 Ω. Only 8 Ω is below it: 50 Ω is the series total, and 25 Ω is half the sum, which only works for two equal resistors.

caption: In series the resistances simply add: the total is bigger than any one of them.

md: For resistors in series the total is the sum, $R = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$, for as many as there are. The total is always bigger than the biggest single resistor.

**Read the figure.**
**Step 1.** Add the first two: 4 + 6 = 10 Ω.
**Step 2.** Add the third: 10 + 10 = 20 Ω between A and B.

prompt: Resistors of 15 Ω, 22 Ω and 33 Ω are connected in series. What is their total resistance, in ohms?
explain: In series every resistor lies on the one route, so each adds its own opposition, just as 4 + 6 + 10 made 20 Ω on the figure. Here 15 + 22 + 33 = 70 Ω.

text: 4. Two equal resistors in parallel: halve one

caption: Two equal routes side by side: half the resistance of one of them.

md: Two **equal** resistors side by side give twice the route for the same voltage, so twice the current, so half the resistance: $R = R_1 \div 2$. The shortcut works only when the two resistors are equal.

**Read the figure.**
**Step 1.** Two 24 Ω resistors: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 Ω.
**Step 2.** Check: 12 Ω is less than 24 Ω. Adding them, 24 + 24 = 48 Ω, would be the series rule.

title: The mark most Foundation candidates lost
md: Summer 2025 Foundation: most candidates found the series total of two 9 Ω resistors, but only the most able found their parallel total. Halve an equal pair; never add it.

prompt: Two 50 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance, in ohms?
explain: Two equal routes carry twice the current of one for the same voltage, so the pair has half the resistance of one resistor, as the two 24 Ω resistors on the figure gave 12 Ω. Here 50 ÷ 2 = 25 Ω, which is less than 50 Ω, as a parallel total must be.

alt: A 20 ohm and a 30 ohm resistor in parallel between terminals A and B, 12 ohms in total.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="p2resun"><title id="p2resun">A 20 ohm and a 30 ohm resistor connected in parallel between terminals A and B: 12 ohms in total</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7"><path d="M134 110 L146 110"/><path d="M254 110 L266 110"/><path d="M146 64 L146 156"/><path d="M254 64 L254 156"/><path d="M146 64 L178 64"/><path d="M222 64 L254 64"/><path d="M146 156 L178 156"/><path d="M222 156 L254 156"/><path d="M178 55 H222 V73 H178 Z"/><path d="M178 147 H222 V165 H178 Z"/></g><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2"></g><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none"><path d="M142.4 110 a3.6 3.6 0 1 0 7.2 0 a3.6 3.6 0 1 0 -7.2 0 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M250.4 110 a3.6 3.6 0 1 0 7.2 0 a3.6 3.6 0 1 0 -7.2 0 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor"><text x="200" y="46" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15">20 Ω</text><text x="200" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15">30 Ω</text></g><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7"><path d="M74 110 L134 110"/><path d="M266 110 L326 110"/></g><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none"><path d="M69.5 110 a4.5 4.5 0 1 0 9 0 a4.5 4.5 0 1 0 -9 0 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M321.5 110 a4.5 4.5 0 1 0 9 0 a4.5 4.5 0 1 0 -9 0 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor"><text x="66" y="116" text-anchor="end" font-size="16" font-weight="600">A</text><text x="334" y="116" font-size="16" font-weight="600">B</text><text x="200" y="226" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="600">between A and B: 12 Ω</text></g></svg>
caption: Unequal resistors in parallel: the total is less than the smaller one.

md: For two **unequal** resistors in parallel, Higher Tier uses $\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2}$. The sum on the right gives $\dfrac{1}{R}$, not R, so the last step is always to turn the answer upside down.

**Read the figure.**
**Step 1.** Write the equation: $\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{30}$
**Step 2.** Common denominator: $\dfrac{3}{60} + \dfrac{2}{60} = \dfrac{5}{60}$
**Step 3.** Turn it upside down: $R = \dfrac{60}{5} = 12$ Ω
**Check:** 20 × 30 ÷ (20 + 30) = 12 Ω, less than 20 Ω.

prompt: A 12 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance, in ohms?
explain: Add the reciprocals, then turn the sum upside down, as the figure's pair did: $\dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{4}{12}$, so R = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 Ω. It is less than 4 Ω, the smaller resistor, as a parallel total must be.

title: Resistors in series and parallel
why: Five minutes on total resistance in series and in parallel, and on using the total to find a current.

title: Made for another board
md: The video follows a board that does not ask for the parallel calculation, so it may only say that a parallel total is less than either resistor. CCEA sets the calculation: sections 4 and 5 are yours to know. Where it says potential difference, CCEA says voltage.

prompt: An 8 Ω resistor and a 24 Ω resistor are connected first in series and then in parallel. Which pair of totals is right?
options: 32 Ω in series, 6 Ω in parallel
32 Ω in series, 16 Ω in parallel
6 Ω in series, 32 Ω in parallel
answer: 32 Ω in series, 6 Ω in parallel
explain: In series the two add, 8 + 24 = 32 Ω. In parallel the total must be below the smaller resistor, 8 Ω: 8 × 24 ÷ 32 = 6 Ω. Halving the sum only works for an equal pair.

caption: Box the parallel pair, replace it by one value, then add along the line.

md: When a circuit has a series part and a parallel part, deal with the parallel section first. Replace the pair by the single resistance it is equivalent to, then add the series resistors along the line. Never add a parallel pair straight into the total.

**Read the figure.**
**Step 1.** The pair, 20 Ω and 30 Ω in parallel: 20 × 30 ÷ 50 = 12 Ω.
**Step 2.** Add the series resistor: 5 + 12 = 17 Ω.

prompt: An 8 Ω resistor is connected in series with two 12 Ω resistors that are in parallel with each other. What is the total resistance, in ohms?
explain: Reduce the parallel pair first, as the boxed pair on the figure was: two equal 12 Ω resistors give 12 ÷ 2 = 6 Ω. Then add along the line: 8 + 6 = 14 Ω. Adding all three, 32 Ω, would treat the pair as if it were in series.

text: 8. Where the parallel equation comes from

alt: A supply of voltage V across two resistors R1 and R2 in parallel; a current I leaves the supply and splits into I1 through R1 and I2 through R2.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 280" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="p2resder"><title id="p2resder">A supply of voltage V across two resistors R1 and R2 in parallel; a current I leaves the supply and splits into I1 through R1 and I2 through R2</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7"><path d="M60 60 L60 240"/><path d="M340 60 L340 240"/><path d="M60 60 L196 60"/><path d="M204 60 L340 60"/><path d="M60 150 L178 150"/><path d="M222 150 L340 150"/><path d="M60 240 L178 240"/><path d="M222 240 L340 240"/><path d="M196 43 L196 77" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M204 52 L204 68" stroke-width="4.2"/><path d="M178 141 H222 V159 H178 Z"/><path d="M178 231 H222 V249 H178 Z"/></g><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none"><path d="M56.4 150 a3.6 3.6 0 1 0 7.2 0 a3.6 3.6 0 1 0 -7.2 0 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M336.4 150 a3.6 3.6 0 1 0 7.2 0 a3.6 3.6 0 1 0 -7.2 0 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M60 111 L55 99 L65 99 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M296 150 L284 155 L284 145 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M296 240 L284 245 L284 235 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor"><text x="200" y="38" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15">supply voltage V</text><text x="44" y="110" text-anchor="end" font-size="15" font-weight="600">I</text><text x="200" y="132" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="600">R1</text><text x="200" y="222" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="600">R2</text><text x="290" y="180" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="600">I1</text><text x="290" y="270" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="600">I2</text></g></svg>
caption: The parallel rules, written in symbols: one voltage V, and a current that splits.

md: The equation follows from the parallel rules and V = I R, so you can rebuild it if you ever forget it.

**Step 1.** The branch currents add up: $I = I_1 + I_2$
**Step 2.** Every branch has the same voltage V, and each current is V over its resistance: $\dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{V}{R_1} + \dfrac{V}{R_2}$
**Step 3.** Divide every term by V: $\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2}$
Series comes out the same way: the voltages add, $IR = IR_1 + IR_2$, and dividing by the one current I gives $R = R_1 + R_2$.

prompt: In the derivation of the parallel equation, why can V be divided out of every term?
options: every branch has the same voltage as the supply across it
the current is the same in every branch
V is always equal to 1 volt
answer: every branch has the same voltage as the supply across it
explain: Step 2 used one V for the whole pair and for each branch, because in parallel every branch is joined straight across the supply. A factor shared by every term can be divided out, leaving the resistances alone. The currents are not the same in each branch; that is why they have to add.

md: **Build a total from given resistors.** Summer 2019 and Summer 2023 Higher gave three resistors and four totals to reach. Try the moves in turn: add in series, halve an equal pair, combine an unequal pair, one in series with a pair.

**Switches.** Summer 2021 Higher and Summer 2022 Foundation: an open switch in a branch removes that branch; a closed switch across a resistor lets the current go round it, so that resistor adds nothing.

**Use your answer to (i), then find the currents.** Summer 2021 Foundation and Higher: combine the pair first and reuse it. Later parts (Summer 2021 and 2023 Higher) share a current between the branches with the parallel rules.

prompt: In the circuit shown, switches K and L are both closed. What is the resistance between X and Y, in ohms?
explain: Take each switch in turn. K closed gives the current a path round the 5 Ω resistor, so it adds nothing. L closed brings the 12 Ω branch in, in parallel with 6 Ω: 6 × 12 ÷ 18 = 4 Ω. That pair is all that is left between X and Y.

md: The hardest version gives the resistors and the total, and asks for the arrangement (Summer 2023 Higher). Work backwards: above every single resistor, something is in series; below the smallest, a parallel pair; in between, one resistor plus a pair.
**Read the figure.** From 4 Ω, 12 Ω, 12 Ω, aim for 15 Ω. Step 1: it is bigger than 12 Ω, so put one 12 Ω in series, leaving 15 − 12 = 3 Ω. Step 2: 4 Ω and 12 Ω in parallel give 48 ÷ 16 = 3 Ω.

title: Where the specification stops
md: CCEA asks for any two resistors in parallel; three or more all in parallel go beyond the specification.

prompt: A pupil has a 4 Ω resistor and two 12 Ω resistors. Which arrangement gives a total of 10 Ω?
options: the 4 Ω resistor in series with the two 12 Ω resistors in parallel
one 12 Ω resistor in series with the 4 Ω and the other 12 Ω in parallel
answer: the 4 Ω resistor in series with the two 12 Ω resistors in parallel
explain: Work backwards from 10 Ω, as the figure did from 15 Ω. Two 12 Ω resistors in parallel give 6 Ω, and 4 + 6 = 10 Ω. A 12 Ω in series with the other pair is the figure's own 15 Ω, and all three in series make 28 Ω.

md:
Add every resistance in series.
Halve an equal pair in parallel.
Combine any two in parallel (Higher): add the reciprocals, then turn the sum upside down.
Reduce a parallel section first, then add along the line.
Check every parallel total: it is less than the smaller resistor.

Resistance totals come as one- to three-mark parts inside a circuit question that goes on to a current with V = I R. For a Higher parallel pair, write the equation first; the last mark is the value after turning it upside down. Stuck? Ask whether the resistors share one route or several, and check a parallel answer against the smaller resistor.
